summary: Defines managed objects for implementations of the Internet Protocol, independent of the IP version. It replaces RFCs 2011, 2465, and 2466 and is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A single standard checklist for asking any device how its internet addressing is doing, for both old and new addresses.

subtitle: One management model for IPv4 and IPv6: the counters, address tables and settings an SNMP manager can read from any IP stack.

tldr.problem: IPv4 and IPv6 each had their own separate management objects (RFC 2011 for IP, RFCs 2465 and 2466 for IPv6), so a manager needed two parallel sets of tables to monitor one node.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4293 defines a single IP-MIB module whose tables carry an address type in their index, so the same statistics, address and neighbor tables describe IPv4 and IPv6 alike, plus new IPv6 tables for default routers and router advertisements.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFCs 2011, 2465 and 2466 and is a Proposed Standard. Not every device implements every table; a compliance section says which groups each kind of entity needs.

facts.label: General knobs
facts.value: 3 (forwarding, TTL or hop limit, reassembly timeout)

today: RFC 4293 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2006. It obsoletes RFC 2011, RFC 2465 and RFC 2466, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Single IP-Version-Independent MIB
sections.content:
RFC 4293 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB), the virtual information store that network management tools read through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). The module is written in SMIv2, the Structure of Management Information, and it covers the Internet Protocol and ICMP in an IP version independent way. Routes are excluded: the module description says it manages IP and ICMP implementations but not IP routes.

The main goal, in the RFC's own revision history, is to create one set of objects to describe and manage IP modules. Earlier, RFCs 2465 and 2466 created objects independent from RFC 2011. This document merges all three into one unified set. A second goal is to make a node running IPv6 easier to manage by adding new objects.

For the first time the counters carry an IP address type in their index, which keeps the information for each IP version separate inside the same table.
sections.eli5: Instead of keeping two notebooks, one for old internet addresses and one for new ones, the memo puts everything in one notebook with a column that says which kind each entry is.

sections.title: The Tables and Groups
sections.content:
The MIB is a small number of single objects plus a series of tables. The general objects are only three "knobs": enable or disable forwarding, set the limit on a packet's lifetime (TTL or hop count), and set the timeout for reassembling fragments. The reassembly timeout exists only for IPv4, because IPv6 specifies that value directly.

The tables cover:

  • Interface tables, one per protocol, with administrative status objects that can be used together with ifAdminStatus to connect an interface to the IPv4 stack, the IPv6 stack or both.
  • Statistics tables for IP and for ICMP.
  • The address prefix table and the address table, which lets a manager learn what addresses the entity thinks it has.
  • The address translation table, which maps IP addresses to physical addresses as formed by ARP for IPv4 or neighbor discovery for IPv6.
  • The IPv6 scope zone index table, the default router table and the router advertisement table.

The RFC adds a warning about multi-stack designs: the MIB gives no native support for several stacks sharing the same address type. One option is to give each stack its own SNMP context.
sections.eli5: The checklist has a few switches you can flip and a set of lists: which doors (interfaces) the machine has, what its addresses are, how much traffic it handled, and who its neighborhood helpers (default routers) are.

sections.title: Traffic Statistics and Counters
sections.content:
Two statistics tables hold the packet counters. ipSystemStatsTable reports system wide totals, indexed by address type alone. ipIfStatsTable reports the same counters per interface, indexed by address type and then interface. The object identifier ipSystemStatsEntry.2 is reserved so that counter numbers line up between the two tables.

The RFC includes a diagram of the order in which counters apply as a packet moves through the stack. Counters such as InReceives, InHdrErrors, InAddrErrors, InDelivers and OutRequests mark steps on the input and output paths, with separate counters for forwarding, fragmentation (OutFragOks, OutFragFails, OutFragCreates) and reassembly (ReasmReqds, ReasmOKs, ReasmFails). Notes on the diagram give counting rules, such as incrementing OutFragFails rather than OutDiscards when fragmenting fails, so that FragOks + FragFails equals FragRqds.

Each row also has a discontinuity time and a refresh rate. The discontinuity object tells a manager if an event, such as a system reinitialization or an interface being cycled, has invalidated its picture of the counters. The refresh rate suggests a polling interval.

ICMP gets two sets of statistics: simple counters for messages and errors, and a per-message-type table indexed by address type and message type. A row for message type X may exist early but must exist after the first message of that type is sent or received.
sections.eli5: The machine keeps tally marks for every packet it receives, sends, throws away or splits up. A note on each tally sheet says when the counting was last reset, so you know if the numbers can still be trusted.

sections.title: Conformance and Compliance
sections.content:
Nobody is expected to implement every object. The conformance section groups objects into units, and the compliance section says which units different entities need. The circumstances it uses are implementing IPv4, IPv6 or IPv6 router functions, and having a bandwidth of less than 20MB, between 20MB and 650MB, or greater than 650MB. The bandwidth split exists because the statistics groups are divided by how fast their counters could wrap within an hour.

Some requirements are stated plainly in the overview:

  • The base system statistics group is mandatory for all entities; the interface-specific statistics groups are optional.
  • The address table, the default router table and both ICMP statistics tables are required for all entities.
  • The address prefix table and the IPv6 scope zone index table are required for IPv6 entities.
  • The router advertisement table is required only for IPv6 router entities.

The MIB also keeps a set of deprecated objects from earlier versions as part of the historical record.
sections.eli5: Small devices do not have to answer every question on the list. The rules say which questions every device must answer and which ones only routers or very fast devices need to handle.

sections.title: Updating Older Implementations
sections.content:
The RFC tells implementers of the old MIBs what changes. Four classes of change are listed: most old objects have new object IDs and extra indexes for the address type; address objects now allow both IPv4 and IPv6, with an address type object; replacement tables gained new objects; and some tables, such as ipIfStatsTable and ipDefaultRouterTable, are entirely new.

For an IPv4-only implementation, ipForwarding, ipDefaultTTL and ipReasmTimeout stay unchanged, and the old counters move to ipSystemStatsTable. For an IPv6 implementation, ipv6Forwarding and ipv6DefaultHopLimit are renamed ipv6IpForwarding and ipv6IpDefaultHopLimit. IPv6 route information was removed from this MIB and left to an update of the IP Forwarding Table MIB (RFC 4292).

One implementation tip: a system may fill ipSystemStatsTable by summing per-interface counters, but then the statistics of a removed interface must be retained.
sections.eli5: If you built a device with the old checklists, this part is the moving guide. It says which old questions got new numbers, which were renamed and which are brand new.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Writable objects are sensitive. The RFC lists several and the harm from changing them. Examples: turning forwarding on or off could deny service or open a conduit into an area; lowering the default TTL or hop limit could cause packets to be discarded before they arrive; changing the address table or the router advertisement table could make a node ignore traffic or disrupt autoconfiguration for all hosts on a link; and changing the address translation objects could divert messages.

Readable objects can matter too. The address table is a convenient list of every address in use by a node, and the RFC notes that an attacker could use it to correlate an RFC 3041 privacy address with known public addresses.

The RFC recommends the security features of SNMPv3, including its authentication and privacy mechanisms, and says that deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The checklist shows private details and has switches that could cause trouble. So only trusted people should be able to look at it or flip the switches, and the memo says to use the strongest SNMP locks.
